claims.text: The initial material is a W–Cu composite containing micron-sized tungsten particles dispersed in a copper matrix without interfacial engineering.
CVD in a CH4/H2 atmosphere at 900–1100 °C can produce a conformal 10–50 nm WC shell on tungsten particles.
The WC-coated tungsten particles can subsequently be consolidated into W–Cu composites by hot pressing or spark plasma sintering.
The proposed coating creates a graded, ultra-thin WC interlayer at the W/Cu interface.
A WC interlayer reduces thermal boundary resistance between tungsten and copper.
The graded WC interface improves phonon transport across the tungsten and copper phases.
The graded WC interface improves electron transport across the tungsten and copper phases.
WC is robust under mechanical stress.
The WC interlayer helps retain the structural integrity of the W–Cu composite under irradiation and mechanical stress.
The WC-interlayered composite will have higher effective thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable uncoated W–Cu composite.
Adding the WC interlayer will cause minimal change in mechanical durability relative to the uncoated control.
Adding the WC interlayer will cause minimal change in irradiation resistance relative to the uncoated control.
An uncoated W/Cu interface has higher thermal boundary resistance than the proposed WC-modified interface.
Higher thermal boundary resistance at the uncoated W/Cu interface causes lower effective thermal conductivity.
The predicted benefits will persist under the high heat flux, mechanical loading, and irradiation regimes relevant to heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications.
Departures from the target coating thickness or uniformity may compromise the predicted performance.
Overreaction during CVD may compromise the predicted performance.
